systemic_fix: Kill @-tag assignment. Every client gets ONE named owner, published in their chat by name, and every commitment made to that client gets written into a dated in-chat ledger with an owner and a due date — closed with 'done, here's the result' or killed with 'we're not doing this, here's why'. Nothing is allowed to simply age out. That single mechanism sits underneath all ten dimensions: follow_through is 3.00 across all nineteen accounts because work assigned by tag in a group chat dies silently the moment the tagged person goes quiet, and the client is the only one who notices. Pair it with two hard gates — no credential ever enters a client group chat, and no fan payment is taken for anything the creator hasn't approved — and one standing weekly outbound per account that contains a number and contains no ask.
team_broadcast:
Team — three changes, effective today, no exceptions.

1. CREDENTIALS. Nobody asks a client for a password, login, or 2FA code in a client group chat, ever again. Not 'send login', not 'direct login would work too'. If you need access, you tell Vivek and he collects it privately. We have live client passwords sitting in seven group chats right now, some of them for months, and people have been added to those chats since. This one is not negotiable.

2. ONE OWNER PER CLIENT. You will be told this week which accounts are yours by name. If it's yours, you read that chat daily and you answer it — no @-tagging someone else and walking away. If you can't own it, say so now and I'll reassign it. Mayson has had to tag colleagues 35 times across two accounts to get them to read their own clients' messages. That stops.

3. PROMISES GET WRITTEN DOWN. Anything you tell a client you'll do goes into that chat with a date on it, and it gets closed out — either 'done, here's the result' or 'we're not doing this, here's why'. Right now we have 350 promises across the book that just quietly died. Not one client in nineteen has a clean record with us on this.

One more thing, and I mean it as praise: Mayson closed a 331-day-old problem for a client in 24 minutes last Friday and apologised for it taking that long. Fred's pause-and-verify rule has run eleven days with zero breaches. Nick has never once missed a weekly DMCA update in twelve months. It works when we do it. We just aren't doing it anywhere near often enough.

Nothing in this message is about working harder. It's about finishing what we start and writing it down. — Derrek
pattern: Speed masks abandonment. Median first reply across the book is minutes — Sarah Lloyd ~7 minutes, Amber Haze ~15, Lauryn ~2 — and responsiveness is the LOWEST-scoring gap dimension at 2.26. But follow_through is a perfect 3.00 across all nineteen clients: we acknowledge instantly and close nothing. The clients themselves have adapted to it in the same way every time — they raise a thing, chase it two or three times, then stop raising it. That stopping is the actual churn signal, and we read it as calm. Liza stopped asking about three deleted accounts. Sarah stopped asking about a 530k IG down 33 days. Sarah Lloyd stopped mentioning a $25k whale. Vale stopped chasing $5,300 of fan orders. Lauryn stopped chasing a Facebook problem she had raised for 349 consecutive days. Every one of them is still paying, which is why nobody noticed. And when the account finally goes, our only reflex is a collections chase — we sent one to Paige seven days after she resigned, and in two of the three earlier churns nobody on our side ever registered the client had left.
